title: Cross-Layer SLO Validation & Benchmark Orchestrator
author: Aisha Patel
content:
Summary:
This document defines the Cross-Layer SLO Validation and Benchmark Orchestrator (CL-SVBO): a reproducible process and reference implementation for validating runtime SLOs end-to-end across scheduler decisions, kernel selection, and system-level telemetry. The goal is to provide a single authoritative workflow teams can run to certify that a code change, kernel rollout, or scheduler tune does not regress production SLOs.

Motivation and scope:
- Problem: We observe regressions that only appear when scheduler heuristics, kernel mappings, and telemetry interact under production-shaped load. Isolated microbenchmarks miss these interactions.
- Scope: CL-SVBO covers testing of latency SLOs, p99/p95 tail behavior, model-variant fallbacks, and degradation policies for the serving runtime. It is intended for: runtime engineers, kernel maintainers, SRE runbook authors, and release managers.

Key concepts (definitions):
1) SLO surface: per-route latency SLO (e.g., p99 <= 120ms for chat-range <512 tokens), throughput SLOs, and error budget burn rate thresholds.
2) Cross-layer signal: correlated observability traces that join scheduler decisions (slot allotment, kernel choice), kernel latency, and application-level token generation time.
3) Benchmark orchestrator: an automation harness that composes traffic shaping, shadowing, and controlled perturbations while recording deterministic traces.

Architecture overview (text diagram):
- Components:
  - runtime-orchestrator: control plane process that triggers experiments and records metadata (git sha, kernel version, scheduler profile).
  - benchmark-agent (fleet): distributed workload generators that mirror production traffic shapes.
  - telemetry-bridge: consumes traces, metric rollups, and scheduler decision logs; produces joinable event streams keyed by request_id.
  - experiment-coordinator: enforces perturbations (kernel slowdowns, affinity changes, NUMA noise).

Behavioral contract:
- Every experiment run produces an artifact with these sections: metadata.yaml, workload_manifest.json, traces.jl (line-delimited JSON), metrics.csv, and a verdict.json summarizing SLO pass/fail with per-bucket contributors.

Configuration table (recommended defaults):
| key | description | default |
|-----|-------------|---------|
| workload_profile | which production traffic shape to emulate (see profiles/*) | medium-burst-chat |
| duration_minutes | how long to run the steady-state portion | 30 |
| kernel_set | list of kernel builds to exercise | [stable, tuned] |
| perturbation | fault injection policy | none |
| collectors | telemetry endpoints to pull (traces, events, metrics) | telemetry-bridge:9411 |

Quick start (runbook):
1) Checkout the orchestrator repo and select the baseline and candidate kernels: git checkout && export BASELINE=stable && export CANDIDATE=experiment-2027-02.
2) Prepare metadata: ./rbench prepare --workload medium-burst-chat --save metadata.yaml
3) Dry-run (no perturbation): ./rbench orchestrate --metadata metadata.yaml --duration 20 --collect-only
4) Perturbation run (scheduler tweak): ./rbench orchestrate --metadata metadata.yaml --duration 30 --perturb scheduler:priority-window=20ms
5) Collect artifacts: ./rbench collect --run-id <id> --out ./artifacts/<run-id>
6) Analyze: ./rbench analyze --artifacts ./artifacts/<run-id> --report ./reports/<run-id>-report.md

Profiling playbook (when an SLO fails):
1) Verify experiment integrity: check metadata.yaml for correct git sha, kernel versions, and that agents were stable for at least the first 5 minutes.
2) Decompose tail: run the decomposition tool to join traces by request_id and produce a per-request timing waterfall. Command: ./rbench analyze --decompose --artifacts ./artifacts/<run-id>
3) Attribution checklist (ordered):
   a) Scheduler decision time: filter events for scheduler.* and compute median and p99 elapsed between arrival and kernel assignment. Threshold: p99 scheduler-decision < 8ms.
   b) Kernel latency: aggregate kernel.exec_ms by kernel_build and sequence_length_bin. Look for >15% increase in p99 vs baseline for specific bins.
   c) KV cache misses: join kvcache.hit=false events. If mis-hit rate > 3% correlating to latency spikes, escalate to model-onboarding.
   d) Network/dispatch noise: verify gRPC send/recv stalls; if present, open network incident and mark run as non-deterministic.
4) If step 3 finds a scheduler-related root cause, reproduce with microbench: a synthetic batch with identical concurrency and sequence bins and CPU/gpu affinity pinned.

Benchmark suite: workload profiles and acceptance gates:
- Profiles (examples):
  - small-chat-burst: 1–4 tokens per request; bursty arrival; target p99 < 30ms.
  - medium-burst-chat: seq_len 128–512, mixed streaming; target p99 < 120ms.
  - long-search: seq_len 512–2048, high KV miss rate; target p99 < 600ms.
- Acceptance gates (automated):
  1) Functional pass: request success rate >= 99.5%
  2) Latency pass: p95 and p99 within configured gates (see profiles/*).
  3) Regression cap: candidate must not exceed baseline p99 by more than 7% for any profile bin.

Release checklist (for kernel/scheduler changes):
1) Run CL-SVBO on baseline and candidate across all three profiles.
2) Run production canary mirroring at 10% traffic with shadow-mode telemetry for 24h.
3) If any SLO gate fails, halt promotion and file incident with tags: runtime-regression, kernel, scheduler, <owner-team>.

Operator runbook (triage steps):
1) Detect: alert fires for p99-sli-breach.<route> with >5% error-budget burn over 1h.
2) Snapshot: trigger ./rbench quick-snapshot --route <route> which launches a 10-minute capture and stores to S3 under artifacts/snapshots/<timestamp>.
3) Correlate: run ./rbench correlate --snapshot <path> --query 'scheduler.* OR kernel.exec_ms OR kvcache.*'
4) Mitigation options (ordered):
   - Revert scheduler profile to last-known-good: runtime-orchestrator apply --profile stable-slo-preserve
   - Pin model-variant to lower-latency quantized build: runtime-orchestrator update-route --route <route> --model <variant-id>
   - Temporarily increase concurrency headroom by scaling dedicated pool: autoscale set --pool <pool-id> --target-util 40%

Metrics and thresholds (extracted):
- p99 latency critical thresholds: small-chat-burst < 30ms, medium-burst-chat < 120ms, long-search < 600ms.
- scheduler-decision p99: 8ms (soft) / 25ms (hard).
- kernel.exec_ms p99 regression cap: +7% over baseline per-bin.
- kvcache miss rate acceptable: <3% correlated to tail events.

Example artifacts (snippets):
- metadata.yaml:
  git_sha: "b1a2c3d4"
  baseline_kernel: "stable-2026-11"
  candidate_kernel: "tuned-priority-42"
  profiles: ["medium-burst-chat"]

- workload_manifest.json (excerpt):
  {
    "profile": "medium-burst-chat",
    "client_concurrency": 120,
    "arrival_pattern": "bursty",
    "seq_len_distribution": {"0-128": 0.2, "128-512": 0.7, "512+": 0.1}
  }

- analysis example (verdict.json):
  {
    "run_id":"2027-02-03-1234",
    "slo_results": {"medium-burst-chat": {"p99": 132.4, "baseline_p99": 119.1, "status":"FAIL", "dominant_cause":"kernel.exec_ms","confidence":0.86}}
  }

Ownership and escalation:
- Owners:
  - runtime-orchestrator: runtime-platform-team@redwood.com
  - scheduler-core: kernel-scheduler-team@redwood.com
  - telemetry-bridge: observability-team@redwood.com
- Escalation path: first responder -> scheduler owner -> runtime team -> SRE -> ENG execs. List oncall rotation lives in people-ops.

Guidelines for experiments that must be suppressed in public artifacts:
- Any run involving customer data or restricted models must be labeled confidentiality:restricted and stored in the private retention bucket. Do not include traces.jl in public decks.

Notes, limitations, and future work:
- CL-SVBO is designed to expose cross-layer interactions but cannot currently simulate under-specified hardware faults (e.g., NVLink partial degrade). A planned extension is the hardware-fault-injector (HFI) shim.
- We are piloting a regression classifier that highlights likely root causes automatically; currently the analyze step is semi-automated and requires human review.

Appendix: common investigation recipes (short):
- Spiking p99 with unchanged kernel: look for scheduler preemption spikes + dispatch queue depth.
- Kernel-specific driver regressions: reproduce with single-agent microbenchmark pinned to the same kernel and CPU/GPU affinity.
- High KV miss correlated tails: reproduce by clearing cache hints and re-running warmup sequences.

Related links and references:
- runtime release checklist: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/runtime-upgrade-validation-and-canary-matrix-2026
- telemetry contract: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/team-wiki/runtime-telemetry-annotation-guidelines-2025

If you are running a CL-SVBO experiment and need help, open a ticket under the "runtime-benchmarking" queue and tag it with the run_id and profile.
